title: Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO
summary:
Last weekend, all hell broke loose around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

On Friday, his intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was made public. Then Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, came to Huang’s home and asked him whether a news report about the relationship was true, according to a person briefed on the interaction. Huang told him it was. By Sunday evening, Huang had publicly apologized for the affair, and Nvidia’s board had said it would investigate his conduct. Teter had to urge directors to do so—the board, which includes executives who’ve known Huang for decades, had been reluctant to act.

In conversations with senior Nvidia executives, Huang maintained that the affair with the woman, Alice Huang, was his only infidelity, according to people familiar with the situation. Had that been the case, perhaps he would have made it through the maelstrom.

title: Commerce Department Finalizing Long-Awaited AI Remote Access Rule
summary:
The Commerce Department is finalizing a long-awaited rule that will prevent Chinese AI firms from remotely accessing advanced AI chips through data centers in other countries, according to two people familiar with the process. The move could help the department push back on criticism that it has acted too slowly to create policies to limit China’s access to advanced AI technologies—rules that have been opposed by influential companies such as Nvidia.

The rule, which could be announced as soon as this month, will expand existing semiconductor-related controls from the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and extend them to seven additional countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to prevent remote access and chip smuggling into China, the people said. Commerce is currently consulting with other government agencies on the rule before it can be finalized, they added.

title: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress Has Tried to Tame Nvidia’s Riskiest Bets
summary:
Nvidia’s appointment Thursday of its longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO will force the finance veteran to guide the business through a fraught storm of uncertainty created by the sudden resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang.

Kress, 59, joined Nvidia in 2013, when the business was a humble supplier of chips for gamers. And while she has played an important role in guiding the company’s ascendance to an all-important place in the AI economy, she wasn’t someone who set the agenda on the company’s major decisions, according to people familiar with Kress.

Huang had run Nvidia with total control—and never established a clear succession plan. One person familiar with Kress said Huang tended to “steamroll” her whenever the two disagreed.

title: Free Chinese AI Can Hack Companies While Frontier Developers Face Diminishing Returns
summary:
Chinese AI that anyone can download for free has become good enough to break into corporate networks, said Ariel Zeitlin, co-founder and chief technology officer of Tenzai, an Israeli startup that sells hacking software for testing corporate defenses, known as continuous penetration testing. 

At the same time, the most advanced AI that had an early lead in cybersecurity capabilities is getting harder and costlier to improve, said Micah Hill-Smith, CEO of AI benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis. That means Chinese models won’t be far behind and makes it unlikely that any one developer pulls far ahead of its rivals.

title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’
summary:
Two centuries after the expedition, Indigenous students are conducting a new wildlife survey along the route

In 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it.

But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

title: Abrupt End to Nvidia’s Jensen Drama Leaves Unanswered Questions
summary:
Jensen Huang’s long-running Nvidia drama ended on a cliffhanger with the news of the CEO’s resignation Thursday morning. We’re going to have to wait a while for the scriptwriters to figure out the next installment of this thriller. At the moment, we’ve got far more questions than answers: What happened between Sunday, when the board said it had confidence in Huang, and Wednesday night when Huang quit (as Nvidia revealed in a securities filing today)? 

What role did the Trump administration play in his departure? Astute watchers of the news media might have noticed that many of the numerous stories about the Wednesday night board meeting called to consider Huang’s future were at least partly written by Washington correspondents not normally reporting on Nvidia’s doings. Was the White House leaking stuff to pressure Huang to go? The answers will eventually come out, to be sure.

title: Jensen Didn’t Create the AI Boom. It Created Him.
summary:
If you follow investors and reporters on X, you would get the sense that the resignation of Jensen Huang amounts to the end of the AI boom. A summary of my X feed Wednesday morning would go something like “I hope the Nvidia board knew what they were doing before ending the world as we know it.”

But if you believe that to be true, you haven’t been paying attention. Because as much as Jensen created the AI boom (and clearly Nvidia’s GPU—the brains that trains AI models—did), the AI boom created Jensen. And that’s key to understanding the world that comes after his reign.

When founder Shay Leighton put fliers in tattoo parlours, barbers and boxing gyms in Australia, men quickly responded – then it went global. But why do some feel such baggage about books?

“When did we decide that men and reading and toughness all had to be separate things?” Shay Leighton asks over a pint of Melbourne Black in his local Brunswick pub. “I don’t know about you, but I didn’t get a vote.”

For 14 years, Leighton has run the Tough Guy Book Club, a not-for-profit charity dedicated to encouraging men to read – although he’s quick to stress that they do more than just that. “We’re not a reading club, we’re a talking club,” he says. “The three goals of book club are: read more, talk more, have more friends.”

title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
summary:
The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country

Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.

title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty-sized landfill
summary:
One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades

As a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents.

The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

Given the popularity of its music and the streaming services’ interest in faith-based programming, I’m always a little surprised that there aren’t more movies and TV shows about Nashville. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. As the days shorten and the temperature cools, children run around a South Carolina camp ground in celebration of the harvest season. For more than 150 years, thousands of people altogether have congregated at St Paul camp ground in Dorchester county. The annual camp meeting serves as a reunion and a place for spiritual kinship for generations of Black families and friends. Gospel groups perform praise dances and sing on the opening night of the weeklong gathering. At night, ministers deliver sermons in an open air structure, before families retreat to their individual wood dwellings arranged in a circle on the grounds. Attendees feast on food common to the region, including fish, wild hog, turkey, alligator and gourds.

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.

Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
summary:
It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world?

‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.

One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. title: Historic US ocean liner sinks near Florida to become world’s largest artificial reef
summary:
SS United States, which set transatlantic speed record during maiden voyage in 1952, is sunk off coast of Destin

The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea, sinking Wednesday off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will begin a new life underwater as an artificial reef.

The nearly 1,000ft American-made vessel, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was launched in 1952 and made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its maiden voyage. The ship carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic over 17 years of operation before being retired in 1969.
